source.title: Towards Safer Large Language Models through Machine Unlearning
source.authors: Zheyuan Liu; Guangyao Dou; Zhaoxuan Tan; Yijun Tian; Meng Jiang

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests unlearning outcomes with harmful-response rates and utility metrics, but does not test whether attacks recover the targeted knowledge.
record.gate_note: The study measures direct responses after unlearning and utility on normal prompts. It does not run recovery attacks. Its fine-tuning baseline trains on safe samples to try to induce forgetting; it is not fine-tuning an already-unlearned model as a recovery attack. The study explicitly says jailbreak robustness is unknown.
record.test_reason: This is a method paper that reports only its own method (SKU) and baselines on harmful-response rate under direct prompts, plus perplexity and BLEURT on normal prompts. It runs no recovery attack of any kind: no relearning, no activation ablation, no quantization, no rephrasing or jailbreak. It also does not measure targeted-knowledge accuracy against chance. The authors state that SKU's robustness to jailbreaks is 'still unknown'. Its results therefore cannot bear on whether unlearning is shallow. The suppression results are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that SKU balances harmful-output reduction against normal-prompt utility better than FT, task-vector and GA baselines, on seen and unseen harmful prompts. They concede it is not best on any single metric, and that its robustness to adversarial attacks such as jailbreaks is unknown.
record.recipe_differences: SKU first acquires harmful knowledge using guided distortion, random disassociation, and preservation divergence, then negates the resulting parameter difference. It also compares with gradient ascent, GA with mismatch, fine-tuning, and a task-vector baseline.
record.method_sensitivity: Model architecture/size and training step; harmful-response and utility outcomes differ by model and method.

fits_no_version.finding: SKU (negating a harmful task vector) cuts GPT-4-judged harmful-response rates on direct harmful prompts from about 54–58% to 3–4% on OPT-2.7B and LLaMA2-7B/13B. Normal-prompt perplexity stays at about 24–25, versus >10^3 for GA and GA+Mismatch, which reach 1–5%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unlearning methods can suppress harmful responses to direct prompts with less utility loss than gradient ascent. This is measured without any recovery attack.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: No recovery attacks are tested. Harmfulness is judged by few-shot GPT-4; the reported utility metrics are perplexity and BLEURT similarity, not a broad capability evaluation. No uncertainty estimates are stated.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row limit. Harmful-perplexity values and additional step-wise plots are omitted because they do not directly test recovery; the paper's own method comparisons are represented by the principal Table 1 outcomes.

untested.parts: Targeted-knowledge accuracy near chance, general-ability benchmarks, and resistance to simple attacks. Only direct-prompt harmful-response rate and perplexity/BLEURT are measured.
All; no relearning fine-tuning of unlearned models.
All; no activation-direction ablation and no blocking-vs-deletion analysis.
All; no rephrasing, jailbreak, language or in-context attacks. Authors say jailbreak robustness is unknown.
SKU is not evaluated against any recovery attack, so no robustness claim is tested.

record.verdict_notes: Classified T6/discusses rather than tests: the record's 'tests' on version A rests on direct-prompt harmful rates, which neither measure knowledge accuracy nor involve any attack. The record's limits_scope label on GA baselines is removed; those are the study's own method comparisons, not a test of shallow unlearning. Table 2 ablations and the step-wise plots likewise bear on no version.

versions.untested_parts: The study measures harmful-response rates rather than targeted-knowledge accuracy, and does not test whether simple attacks recover knowledge.
No post-unlearning recovery fine-tuning on unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten-fact examples.
No activation-direction ablation or test of whether unlearning blocks access rather than deleting knowledge.
No prompt rephrasing, jailbreak, language, or in-context recovery test.
SKU is not evaluated against the recovery attacks in the claim; the paper says jailbreak robustness remains unknown.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Gradient-ascent baselines across the three tested models
reader_labels.reason: Low harmful-response rates coincide with very poor normal-prompt utility (r15–r16, r19–r20, r23–r24), so the unlearning/utility trade-off depends on method.
